title: Brahma medhayā: the second trisuparṇa
theme: The second trisuparṇa: brahman, the sweet, is reached through medhā; prayers to Savitṛ to send good and drive away evil; the ‘honey’ verses asking that the whole world be sweet; and the brāhmaṇa lines on its giving and recitation.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «यद्ब्रह्म सर्वजगत्कारणं सर्ववेदान्तवेद्यं तन्मेधया गुरूपदिष्टमहावाक्यतदर्थधारणशक्त्या लभ्यतामिति शेषः» — brahman, the cause of the world, is to be gained by medhā

sandhi.rule: The visarga of savitaḥ stands for r, which shows before a voiced consonant.

sandhi.type: t before m; e before a vowel
sandhi.rule: tat + me → tan me (P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा)); me + āsuva → ma āsuva: e becomes ay and the y drops (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
-āḥ loses its visarga before a vowel (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
In the Veda a final -n after ā before a vowel becomes ṃ (P. 8.3.9 (दीर्घादटि समानपादे)); the Ṛgveda has madhumāṁ astu.
The visarga after ī becomes r before a voiced consonant.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a

sandhi.rule: brāhmaṇāḥ + trisuparṇam → brāhmaṇās trisuparṇam: the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)).
ā and sahasrāt are written as one; final t stays before p.

morphology.note: adya ‘today’ with its final vowel lengthened, as often in the Ṛgveda; the anonymous commentator glosses it ‘on this day’.
An s-aorist of √sū without augment, used as a request (‘send!’); the anonymous commentator: «सावीः प्रेरय».
The text prints madhu mān no, with a space, for madhumān no; the words are the same as in the Ṛgveda and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (see parallels).

translation.literal: Brahman by medhā; sweetness by medhā; brahman itself, sweetness, by medhā. Today, god Savitṛ, impel for us good fortune with offspring; drive away what comes of bad dreams. All evils, god Savitṛ, drive away; what is good, that send to me. Sweetly [blow] the winds for one who seeks the right order; the rivers pour sweetness; sweet be the plants for us. Sweet [be] the night and the dawn; full of sweetness the earthly region; sweet be the sky, our father. Full of sweetness for us be the tree, full of sweetness be the sun; sweet be the cows for us. Whoever gives this trisuparṇa unasked to a brāhmaṇa — these truly destroy [the sin of] killing an embryo. The brāhmaṇas who recite the trisuparṇa attain soma. They purify the row up to a thousand. Om.
translation.readable: Brahman is reached through understanding; the sweet is reached through understanding; Brahman itself, the sweet, through understanding. Savitṛ, give us today good fortune and descendants, and send away whatever bad dreams bring. Send away every wrong, Savitṛ, and send me what is good. May the winds blow sweetly for one who seeks the true order; may the rivers flow sweet; may the plants be sweet for us; sweet the night and the dawn, sweet the dust of the earth, sweet the sky, our father; sweet the trees, sweet the sun, sweet the cows. The text adds that those who teach this unasked destroy the sin of killing the unborn, that its reciters attain soma, and that they purify a row of a thousand at the meal. Om.

anvaya: ब्रह्म मेधया [लभ्यताम्] । मधु मेधया । ब्रह्मम् एव मधु मेधया । देव सवितः, अद्या नः प्रजावत् सौभगम् सावीः । दुष्ष्वप्नियम् परा सुव । देव सवितः, विश्वानि दुरितानि परासुव । यत् भद्रम् तत् मे आसुव । ऋतायते वाताः मधु [वान्तु] । सिन्धवः मधु क्षरन्ति । ओषधीः नः माध्वीः सन्तु । नक्तम् उत उषसि मधु [अस्तु] । पार्थिवम् रजः मधुमत् [अस्तु] । नः पिता द्यौः मधु अस्तु । वनस्पतिः नः मधुमान् [अस्तु] । सूर्यः मधुमान् अस्तु । गावः नः माध्वीः भवन्तु । यः इमम् त्रिसुपर्णम् अयाचितम् ब्राह्मणाय दद्यात्, एते वै भ्रूणहत्याम् घ्नन्ति । ये ब्राह्मणाः त्रिसुपर्णम् पठन्ति ते सोमम् प्राप्नुवन्ति । [ते] आ सहस्रात् पङ्क्तिम् पुनन्ति । ओम् ।
syntax: Three verbless statements with medhayā (the verb ‘is reached’ supplied); then imperatives to Savitṛ (sāvīḥ, parā … suva, parāsuva, āsuva) with the relative clause yad bhadram; then a string of wishes with madhu/mādhvīḥ/madhumat as predicates and imperatives of √as and √bhū, some verbs supplied. The brāhmaṇa part has a singular relative (yaḥ … dadyāt) taken up by a plural (ete … ghnanti).

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa supply ‘is to be gained’ (brahman is gained by the power to retain the teaching); Bhāskara reads ‘is reached or known by a special understanding’, and the following verses as a prayer for that understanding («अथ तादृशीं मेधां प्रार्थयते»).

The anonymous commentator reads each wish as a prayer that nothing — wind, water, food, time, place — hinder the student’s learning; Bhāskara says the honey here is knowledge of the self («अत्राप्यात्मज्ञानं मधु»).
The killing of an unborn child (of a brāhmaṇa or a king: the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa) or of a brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda (Bhāskara).

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Prose formulas; then gāyatrī verses (Bhāskara: «अद्या न इति द्वे गायत्र्यौ», «मधु वाता ऋतायत इति तिस्त्रो गायत्र्यः»), and the brāhmaṇa in prose.

beginner: The second trisuparṇa opens by saying that Brahman — which is also called ‘the sweet’ — is reached through medhā, the power to take in a teaching and hold on to it. Then it prays to Savitṛ, the god who sets things moving: give us good fortune today, drive away what bad dreams bring, drive away every wrong, send me what is good. The best-known lines follow, the ‘honey verses’: may the winds blow sweetly, the rivers flow sweet, the plants be sweet; sweet the night and the dawn, the earth, the sky our father, the trees, the sun, the cows. The old commentator reads all this as a student’s prayer that nothing in the world get in the way of learning. It ends, like the first, with the text’s own promises to those who teach and recite it.
analogy: Like a student who asks, before an exam, for a quiet room, a clear head, good food and no bad news.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That brahman, the sweet, is reached by medhā; it asks Savitṛ to send good fortune and drive evils away; it wishes that winds, rivers, plants, night and dawn, earth, sky, trees, sun and cows be sweet; and it states the reward of giving and reciting the trisuparṇa.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the power to retain the great sayings taught by the teacher and their meaning, by which brahman is gained: «तन्मेधया गुरूपदिष्टमहावाक्यतदर्थधारणशक्त्या लभ्यतामिति शेषः». Bhāskara: brahman is reached or known by a special understanding («मेधाविशेषेण प्राप्यते ज्ञायते वा»), and the verses that follow ask for it.

commentary.q: Why pray for sweet winds and rivers?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: a strong wind brings illness and hinders knowledge, so its favour is asked, and the same holds for each wish that follows: «प्रबले तु वायौ रोगोत्पत्त्या तत्त्वज्ञानविघ्नः संपद्यतेऽतः स मा भूदिति वायोरानुकूल्यं प्रार्थ्यते». Bhāskara: here too the honey is knowledge of the self: «अत्राप्यात्मज्ञानं मधु».

commentary.q: Where are the Savitṛ verses explained?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara both say these verses were explained earlier in their texts: Sāyaṇa refers to the anuvāka aṇor aṇīyān («अद्या नो देवेत्या कमृक्पञ्चकमणोरणीयानित्यनुवाके व्याख्यातम्»), Bhāskara, who calls them two gāyatrīs («अद्या न इति द्वे गायत्र्यौ»), to the passage beginning ‘uta naḥ priyā’.

commentary.q: What sin does this trisuparṇa remove?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The killing of an unborn child: «ब्राह्मणगर्भस्य राजगर्भस्य वा हननं भ्रूणहत्या» (the anonymous commentator); Bhāskara: the killing of a brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda and its auxiliaries («वेदवेदाङ्गविदो ब्राह्मणस्य वधः»). The anonymous commentator later ranks the three: brahmahatyā is grave, bhrūṇahatyā graver, vīrahatyā gravest (10.41).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. The anonymous commentator reads the bad dream as the appearance of duality («द्वैतप्रतिभासं»), an Advaita reading he gives in passing; Bhāskara reads the honey as knowledge of the self. Neither argues against another school, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

parallels.quote: मधु वाता ऋतायते मधु क्षरन्ति सिन्धवः
parallels.note: The first honey verse is Ṛgveda 1.90.6.
The second; the Ṛgveda reads uṣasaḥ where this text has uṣasi.

parallels.quote: मधु वाता ऋतायते मधु क्षरन्ति सिन्धवः
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka uses the same three verses, interleaved with the Sāvitrī, in the rite of the mantha.

contemporary.text: The commentator reads a hymn about sweet winds and sweet water as a list of what a student needs: health, food, rest, a safe place, no disturbing news. Learning depends on conditions, not only on effort. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you could ask for one thing to be ‘sweet’ around you so that you could learn better, what would it be?
reflect.deeper: Bhāskara says the honey is knowledge of the self. What changes if everything in the world is asked to be sweet for the sake of knowing?
reflect.practice: Before study, set out what you need — water, light, quiet — as the hymn does, one item at a time.

references.text: Sāyaṇa (his 49) and Bhāskara (his 49) comment on this anuvāka; the concordance maps both correctly. The Savitṛ verses are also Ṛgveda 5.82.4–5, which the edition’s parallel sources do not contain.
The effects claimed for giving and reciting the trisuparṇa are the text’s own and are reported as such.

flags.note: medhayā ‘by medhā’ with a supplied verb: gained by it (anonymous, Sāyaṇa) or known by it (Bhāskara).
